newsitem.title: USA: Helms-Burton remains U.S.-Canada thorn. [CORRECTED 22:31 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Helms-Burton remains U.S.-Canada thorn. [CORRECTED 22:31 GMT]

text.p: The United States and Canada on Tuesday sought to emphasize common concerns over Cuba's human rights record but a deep disagreement over America's anti-Cuba sanctions law continued to mar bilateral ties.

At a brief press conference with U.S. Secrtetary of State Madeleine Albright, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said his government would again co-sponsor with Washington this year a U.N. Human Rights Commission resolution faulting Cuba's human rights record.

But later, he told reporters despite sharing the U.S. goal of a "more open pluralistic system" in Cuba, the controversial U.S. anti-Cuba sanctions law called Helms-Burton is causing a "real disruption" in the larger world trading system.

Axworthy was in Washington to work out details of a visit here early next month by Canadian Prime Minister Jean (corrects from Raymond) Chretien with President Clinton. Among the issues on the agenda was Haiti. The U.N. peacekeeping mission in that Caribbean country, which is heavily funded by the United States and Canada, is expected to end no later than July 31.

Axworthy said there is "still a major question mark" over what initiatives can be taken after the U.N. leaves to ensure the stability of Haiti's democratic regime but he hopes the United States and Canada can agree on a joint approach by the time of the Chretien-Clinton meeting.

Canada, Europe and the United States have been at odds over Cuba since Congress, with Clinton's backing, last March passed Helms-Burton after four American citizens flying in light aircraft were shot down over international waters by Cuban jet fighters.
The law allows naturalized Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreigners deemed to have benefited from property confiscated by Cuba since the communist revolution in 1959.

Although this section has twice been suspended by Clinton, another section -- now in effect -- allows Washington to ban executives, shareholders, and representatives investing in companies investing in confiscated property.

At the press conference, Albright stressed the positive, saying the overriding U.S.-Canadian common interest is "the extent to which we agree on the goals, which is a democracy, or movement toward democracy in Cuba."

Axworthy insisted -- gently -- that Canada's attempt to engage Cuba on dialogue on human rights, including his own recent visit and follow-up talks last week, have "made some headway in a couple of crucial areas."
But Albright said despite Axworthy's claims, "I'm sure that he along with the United States is waiting for more concrete results from (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro."
Later, talking to reporters outside the State Department without Albright at his side, Axworthy was asked if the United States and Canada had found more common ground on Cuba.

"We want to work in a way that would reinforce developments, transition, change in Cuba but we'll do it each in our own particular way. We're doing so not in any atmosphere of anomousity. We just agree we've got a different approach coming out of our background and history," he said.

But he acknowledged continued "big difficulties" over Helms-Burton, saying the U.S. refusal to cooperate with a World Trading Organization effort to adjudicate the sanctions law dispute "confirms my own anxiety that Helms-Burtom is causing a real disruption in the larger trading system."

"It does set a real turbulence as we're seeing over the dispute on WTO applications. That's something we've all worked almost a decade to bring about, which is an effective world trading system with a set of rules, which is going to be thrown off track by Helms-Burton," Axworthy said.

The European Union has brought the dispute to the WTO. But last month, Washington challenged the fitness of the WTO to adjudicate the dispute and said it would not cooperate with the WTO investigative panel in this case.
